Back when I had an HP 7475a I remember the order of the vectors drawn was defined by the order of the source file. It had no optimization at all if the program plotting to it did not. Modern pen plotters have drivers that can rearrange the vectors by location, color, layer or other properties to more efficiently save pen movements. My laser cutter which is also vector driven rearranges the vectors to make sure interior cuts on a design are done before exterior/perimeter cuts are made so the material does not fall once cut free from the matrix and shift position if it still needs to cut more vectors. But these of course are modern examples and this IBM plotter probably just went with the order from the plot file.

It was drawing actual lines with an actual pen; most home printers these days use jets of ink and only draw dots.

Pen plotters "print" using vectors instead of a raster (side-to-side scanning) motion like inkjet printers do. Vectors are line segments and curves that are defined by their position in an X-Y grid. They can scale to any size and not lose information like a JPG image would. Because vectors are defined in a more mathematical sense, the plotter software arranges them in a somewhat optimized order to allow the pen mechanism to move around less randomly. This optimization is sometimes thrown off by the order the software that created the vector image used in storing the location information. This causes the plotter to move around seemingly erratically like this video appears to show. I can't tell if there was any optimization in the vector order or if this is simply the order in the image file taking over. Either way it seems to be very sub-optimal.
